entry: Competition to determine the world champion in [[Chess|chess]]. The first event recognized as a world championship was the 1886 match won by Wilhelm Steinitz over Johannes Zukertort. Until 1946 the champion set the terms, and challengers had to defeat him in a match. After Alexander Alekhine's death, the International Chess Federation (FIDE) took over, and a rival title existed from 1993 until the titles were unified in 2006. Matches have been held every two years since 2014. Emanuel Lasker held the title for 27 years, the longest reign. Gukesh Dommaraju defeated Ding Liren in 2024.

Specialized agency of the [[United Nations]] that coordinates responses to international [[Public health|public health]] issues and emergencies. Headquartered in [[Geneva]], Switzerland, it was established on April 7, 1948, and incorporated the assets and duties of the League of Nations' Health Organization. Its stated purpose is to achieve the highest possible level of health for all people, defined as complete physical, mental and social well-being. It promotes the control of epidemic and endemic diseases and sets international standards for biological products. It played a leading role in the eradication of [[Smallpox|smallpox]] and the near-eradication of [[Polio|polio]], and helped develop an [[Ebola]] vaccine. Its current priorities include [[HIV/AIDS]], Ebola, malaria and tuberculosis, as well as heart disease and cancer. It is governed by the World Health Assembly, whose member states elect an executive board. It is funded mainly by member states' contributions.

Landmark or area of outstanding value to humanity, protected under an international [[Treaty|treaty]] administered by [[UNESCO]]. Sites may be ancient ruins, historical structures, [[City|cities]], [[Desert|deserts]], [[Forest|forests]], [[Island|islands]], [[Lake|lakes]], monuments, [[Mountain|mountains]] or wilderness areas, and may represent either a remarkable human accomplishment or a place of great natural beauty. A host country nominates each site, and the UNESCO World Heritage Committee selects those that are unique, identifiable and under sufficient legal protection. The program rests on the Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage, adopted by UNESCO on November 16, 1972. The committee has 21 states parties elected by the United Nations General Assembly. Since then 196 states have ratified the convention. As of July 2026 the list included 1,273 sites in 173 countries.

Annual best-of-seven championship series between the American League (AL) and National League (NL) champions of [[Major League Baseball]]. Teams qualify through a postseason tournament. First played in 1903, it is traditionally held in October and is often called the Fall Classic. The winner receives the Commissioner's Trophy. The series has been contested 122 times through 2026, with the AL winning 68 and the NL 54. The most recent series was won by the [[Milwaukee]] Brewers, who defeated the Tampa Bay Rays in five games.

Complex of seven office buildings in the Financial District of [[Manhattan|Lower Manhattan]], [[New York City]], dedicated in 1973. Its Twin Towers, designed by Minoru Yamasaki, were the tallest buildings in the world when completed. The complex was built to stimulate urban renewal. On [[September 11 attacks|September 11, 2001]], hijackers affiliated with [[Al-Qaeda|al-Qaeda]] flew two jets into the towers, and both collapsed. The attacks killed 2,606 people in and around the towers and all 157 people aboard the two aircraft. A memorial and museum now stand on the site.

Intergovernmental organization regulating and facilitating [[International trade|international trade]]. Established on January 1, 1995, under the 1994 [[Marrakesh|Marrakesh Agreement]], it succeeded the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and has 166 members, representing over 98 percent of world trade. Headquartered in [[Geneva]], [[Switzerland]], it provides a framework for negotiating trade agreements and resolves disputes among members. Its agreements cover goods, services and [[Intellectual property|intellectual property]]. The organization operates on the principle of non-discrimination, with exceptions for environmental protection and national security. Economic studies generally find that it has boosted trade. Critics argue that its benefits are not shared equally, that its agreements may disadvantage developing countries, and that commercial interests have been prioritized over environmental and labor concerns. The Doha Development Round has stalled. Its Secretariat has been led since 2021 by Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala of [[Nigeria]].

Human losses in [[World War II]], the deadliest military conflict in history. Total deaths are estimated at 60–75 million, including those from famine and disease, or about 3 percent of the 2.3 billion world population in 1940. Deaths directly caused by the war were 50–56 million, with 50–55 million civilians and 21–25 million military personnel. More than half of all deaths occurred in the Republic of China and the [[Soviet Union]]. Russian government figures put Soviet losses within postwar borders at 26.6 million. The People's Republic of China puts its war dead at 20 million, and Japan's government gives 3.1 million. Estimates are disputed.

Global system of linked hypertext documents and other resources accessed over the [[Internet]]. Invented by English computer scientist [[Tim Berners-Lee]] at [[CERN]] in 1989, it was opened to the public in 1993 and conceived as a "universal linked information system." Resources are identified by [[URL|uniform resource locators]] and transferred using [[HTTP]]. The original document type is the web page, written in [[HTML]], which supports text, images, video, audio and scripts. Users follow hyperlinks with [[Web browser|web browsers]] to move among resources, and a [[Website|website]] is a group of resources under a common domain name. Berners-Lee had a working browser and server by the end of 1990. The Web has become the dominant information system, used by billions of people.

Global system of production, consumption, trade and financial transactions across all nations. Until the middle of the 19th century, global output was dominated by [[China]] and [[India]], but the [[Industrial Revolution]] in Western Europe and North America shifted the balance toward the Western Hemisphere. As of 2026, 12 countries and two collectives, including the [[African Union]] and the [[European Union]], each account for at least 2.0 percent of world output measured by [[Gross domestic product|gross domestic product]] in nominal or [[Purchasing power parity|purchasing power parity]] terms. Between 1820 and 2000 global income inequality rose by almost 50 percent, mostly before 1950, and has declined since peaking in the 1970s. A study by United Nations University found that the richest 1 percent of adults owned 40 percent of global assets in the 2000s. The global economy shrank 3.4 percent in 2020 during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] and rebounded by an estimated 5.5 percent in 2021.

Totality of existing entities, customarily viewed in [[Philosophy|philosophy]] as all of [[Existence|existence]] or the whole of [[Reality|reality]]. The term is also used more narrowly for the [[Earth]] and all life on it, or for the whole of human existence. Theories of modality treat possible worlds as complete and consistent ways that things could have been. Theology conceptualizes the world in relation to God, as God's creation or as identical to God. The English word comes from [[Old English]] *weorold*, meaning roughly "age of man." Cosmogony studies the world's origin, and eschatology studies its end.

Map of most or all of the surface of [[Earth]]. Maps of a globe necessarily distort it, and world maps reach the extremes of this distortion. From [[Prehistory|prehistory]] through the [[Middle Ages]], an accurate world map was impossible because less than half of Earth's coastlines were known to any culture. Most coastlines were mapped by the mid-1700s and continental interiors by the twentieth century. Political maps emphasize boundaries, physical maps show terrain, and geological maps show underlying rock and faults. The best-known projection is the [[Mercator projection]], originally designed as a nautical chart.

Massively multiplayer online role-playing [[Video game|video game]] released in 2004 for [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]] and [[MacOS|macOS]]. Developed and published by Blizzard Entertainment, it is set in the Warcraft universe on the fictional planet Azeroth. Players create characters, complete quests and engage in player versus player combat. It peaked at 12 million subscribers in 2010 and had over 100 million registered accounts by 2014. By 2017 it had grossed over $9.23 billion. It has had eleven major expansion packs. A vanilla version, World of Warcraft: Classic, launched in 2019. Gaming journalists have cited it as the greatest MMORPG of all time.

Ideal of lasting peace within and among all peoples and nations on Earth. Various [[Religion|religions]] and secular organizations have sought world peace through [[Human rights|human rights]], education, technology, [[Medicine|medicine]] and [[Diplomacy|diplomacy]]. Since 1945 the [[United Nations]] and the five permanent members of its Security Council have aimed to resolve conflicts without war, though numerous conflicts have occurred since. [[Ayn Rand|Ayn Rand]] argued that [[Capitalism|capitalism]] gave humanity its longest period of peace, from 1815 to 1914, although the evidence for capitalist peace is inconclusive. Democratic peace theory holds that democracies rarely or never wage war against each other, although wars between democracies have occurred, such as the Kargil War. Economic norms theory, developed by Michael Mousseau, links impersonal market economies with permanent peace.

Total number of living humans on Earth. The [[United Nations]] estimated that the population exceeded 8 billion on November 15, 2022, and it is about 8.3 billion as of 2026. Growth has been continuous since the end of the [[Black Death]] in 1350, when the population was nearly 370 million. Annual growth peaked at 2.1 percent between 1965 and 1970 and fell to 1.1 percent between 2015 and 2020. The UN projects 9 to 10 billion people by 2050, but other demographers expect decline in the second half of the 21st century if [[Fertility|fertility]] keeps falling.

Large global exhibition showcasing the achievements of nations, also called a universal exhibition. Such fairs typically run for three to six months at one site. The first, in 1791, was held in [[Prague]], in [[Bohemia]]. The 1851 Great Exhibition in London's Crystal Palace is a landmark event. Since the 1928 convention, the Paris-based Bureau International des Expositions (BIE) has sanctioned four types of international exhibition: World Expos, Specialized Expos, horticultural expos and the [[Milan]] Triennial. Fairs have passed through three eras: industrialization, roughly 1850 to 1938; cultural exchange, 1939 to 1987; and nation branding, from 1988. Early fairs first presented inventions such as the [[Telephone|telephone]]. [[Osaka]], Japan, held the most recent World Expo in 2025.

Fundamental cognitive orientation of an individual or society toward the [[World|world]] and its workings. It encompasses an essential part of an individual's or society's [[Knowledge|knowledge]], [[Culture|culture]] and point of view, and may include natural philosophy, fundamental existential and normative postulates, and themes, values, emotions and [[Ethics|ethics]]. When two parties observe the same phenomenon, differing worldviews can lead them to perceive different elements and reach different conclusions. The term is a calque of the German *Weltanschauung*, a concept first used by [[Immanuel Kant]] and later popularized by Hegel. In 1911 the philosopher Wilhelm Dilthey distinguished three recurring types of worldview: naturalism, the idealism of freedom and objective idealism.

Hypothetical structure that connects disparate points in [[Spacetime|spacetime]], visualized as a tunnel. Wormholes are based on a special solution of the [[Einstein field equations]] and are consistent with [[General relativity|general relativity]]. The term was used by American physicist John Archibald Wheeler in a 1957 paper with Charles W. Misner, though Hermann Weyl had proposed a related idea in 1928. In 1995 Matt Visser suggested that negative-mass cosmic strings from the early universe might indicate many wormholes. Physicists such as Kip Thorne have suggested that wormholes can be created artificially. Traversable wormholes would require exotic matter, and they have no direct observational evidence.

Act of religious devotion usually directed toward a [[Deity|deity]], spirit or other supernatural entity. Worship may be performed individually, in a group or by a designated leader, and for many people it is less an emotion than the recognition of its object. The English word derives from [[Old English]] *weorþscipe*, meaning worth-ship, or giving worth to something. Forms include ancestor worship, animal worship, nature worship and pole worship, as well as imperial cults. In [[Buddhism]], devotion takes many forms, including offerings, bowing and chanting, while meditation is a central form of worship. In [[Christianity]], worship is reverent honor paid to God; the [[New Testament]] word *proskuneo* means to bow down. The Mass is the central act of divine worship in the [[Catholic Church]].

Disruption of or damage to living tissue, such as [[Skin|skin]], mucous membranes or organs. Wounds may result from sudden trauma, whether mechanical, thermal or chemical, or develop slowly from disease processes such as [[Diabetes|diabetes]]. Acute wounds result from direct trauma and heal along an expected timeline, while chronic wounds can persist for months. Open wounds break the skin and expose underlying tissue. They include incisions from clean, sharp objects, lacerations caused by [[Blunt trauma|blunt trauma]], abrasions that scrape away the epidermis, and [[Gunshot wound|gunshot wounds]]. Healing normally passes through hemostasis, [[Inflammation|inflammation]], proliferation and tissue remodeling, which typically lasts 12 months but can continue for up to two years. Age, tissue oxygenation, stress, underlying conditions and some medications affect healing, so wounds should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.

1890 massacre of Lakota people by U.S. Army troops at Wounded Knee Creek in [[South Dakota]]. Settlers feared the Ghost Dance signified a dangerous [[Sioux]] resurgence, and troops moved to disarm the camp on December 29, 1890. During the disarmament a rifle discharged, and the firing became indiscriminate. Between 250 and 300 Lakota were killed and 51 wounded, while 25 soldiers died. Nineteen soldiers received the Medal of Honor for the action, which the National Congress of American Indians condemned in 2001. In 1990 both houses of Congress expressed "deep regret" for the massacre.

Family of mostly small marine ray-finned fishes, many of them brightly colored. The family Labridae includes hundreds of species, most of them in tropical and subtropical waters of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans, often near [[Coral reef|coral reefs]]. Most species are less than 20 cm long, although the humphead wrasse can reach 2.5 m. Efficient carnivores, wrasses feed on small [[Invertebrate|invertebrates]], and many follow larger fish to catch the prey they disturb. Many species change sex, and the largest adults become territory-holding males. Their jaw structure has made wrasses a primary study species in fish-feeding [[Biomechanics|biomechanics]]: a loop of four rigid bones allows different arrangements to produce the same result. The humphead wrasse is listed as Endangered because of its slow growth and high market value.

Family of small brown passerine birds, nearly all restricted to the [[New World]]. The family has 19 genera, and the Eurasian wren is the only Old World species. Most wrens are visually inconspicuous but have loud, complex songs, although the larger members of the genus Campylorhynchus can be bold. They have short, usually barred wings and often hold their tails upright. Wrens eat mainly insects, spiders and other small [[Invertebrate|invertebrates]], and some also eat plant matter or small frogs and lizards. A [[Fable|fable]] known since Aristotle names the wren king of birds, because it hid in an eagle's plumage and rode it to the highest altitude. The family name Troglodytidae means "cave-dweller," reflecting the foraging habits of some species in dark crevices. Plumage shows no [[Sexual dimorphism|sexual dimorphism]], and young birds differ little from adults.

[[Martial arts|Martial art]] and combat sport in which competitors grapple to gain advantage through throws, takedowns, joint locks and pins. The best-known form is [[Professional wrestling|professional wrestling]], a type of athletic theater. Other competitive forms include Olympic Greco-Roman and freestyle wrestling, as well as folk and submission wrestling. Wrestling first appeared at the [[Ancient Olympic Games|ancient Olympic Games]] in 708 BC and has been an event at every modern Olympic Games since 1904. Its origins go back around 15,000 to 17,000 years, to cave drawings in [[France]]. In [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]], philosophers including [[Plato]] and [[Socrates]] practiced wrestling, and many of Plato's dialogues are set in wrestling schools. The first organized national tournament in the United States was held in [[New York City]] in 1888.

Single-place biplane that made the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air [[Airplane|airplane]]. Built by the [[Wright brothers]], it flew on December 17, 1903, near Kitty Hawk, [[North Carolina]]. It was powered by a 12-horsepower (9 kW) gasoline engine that drove two propellers. Its wing warping made it relatively unstable. The brothers flew it four times, and the last flight covered 852 ft (260 m) before gusts wrecked it. Orville later restored it. The Flyer joined the [[Smithsonian Institution]] in 1948 and is now displayed at the National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C.

American [[Aviation|aviation]] pioneers who built and flew the first successful powered [[Airplane|airplane]]. Their 1903 [[Wright Flyer]] made the first controlled, sustained flight of an engine-powered, heavier-than-air aircraft, near Kill Devil Hills, [[North Carolina]]. Their key invention was a three-axis control system that let the pilot steer and balance the aircraft, and it remains standard on airplanes. Unlike other experimenters who emphasized engine power, they focused on pilot control and used a small home-built wind tunnel to collect more accurate data. Their 1904 Flyer II made longer flights, including the first circle, and the 1905 Flyer III was the first truly practical [[Fixed-wing aircraft|fixed-wing aircraft]]. They learned mechanics in a [[Dayton, Ohio|Dayton, Ohio]] shop that worked on printing presses and bicycles, and they conducted [[Glider (aircraft)|glider]] tests from 1900 until 1903.
